synthesis: The perspectives concern policy capability, execution timing and orchestration. New papers add more concrete choices inside those categories: ImageWAM and LaWAM change the intermediate used for action prediction, while Rolling-WAM distributes joint denoising across successive updates.

The synthesis calls for comparing complete execution loops, with their observation interfaces, startup costs, steady-state timing and recovery behavior visible. A compact predictive policy is not automatically a replacement for a supervisor or fast controller. These studies support scoped comparisons rather than a universally best architecture.

The new papers distinguish what prediction contributes: editing caches in ImageWAM, latent subgoals in LaWAM, rolling video-action context in Rolling-WAM, and explicit action-plan refinement in LeWAM. They do not measure the same use of a world model.

The synthesis separates training-time gains from decision-time costs. LeWAM’s planning updates candidate actions while keeping model parameters frozen; its physical-robot evaluations use direct execution under a different protocol. Match goal information, task conditions and runtime budgets before treating results as evidence for adding online planning.

The papers broaden representation beyond a coordinate choice. H2R-Bridge separates observation alignment from action decoding; GLAM grounds latent actions with target-robot supervision. H2RBench holds robot supervision fixed and finds that more human data has task- and method-dependent value.

The synthesis accounts for for coverage, interfaces and evaluation separately. Scale Up Strategically adds another question: which demonstrations should receive a fixed collection budget? Transfer evidence should retain its robot-data budget, environment assumptions and scoring definition; a weighted task-progress score should not become a binary success percentage.

The papers show different ways to use an existing model. RARA preserves representations using relevant retrieved trajectories; Memory Anchors selects replay states for retaining earlier tasks; MuSe adds force-torque observations while replaying original data. Those mechanisms spend additional data and compute in different places.

The synthesis starts with identifying the actual bottleneck and account for the whole update budget. RARA’s extra alignment stage and access to relevant pretraining data matter; selective replay still needs diversity. These results motivate targeted adaptation and retention tests, rather than a single ranking of pretraining, post-training and corrections.

The central takeaway is to prioritize a measured deployment-to-learning loop as the key strategic advantage across architectures. Russ Tedrake’s factory discussion connects productive deployments, intervention records and postmortems to concrete learning needs. This synthesis places that capability ahead of choosing a single winning architecture: real experience becomes useful when it feeds data selection, targeted learning and validated updates. That prioritization is an editorial judgment about where to invest, rather than a universal empirical ranking of companies or robot systems.

Observations alone do not improve a policy. FAR makes the supervision contract visible through human outcome labels in its physical tests; ContactGuard contributes failure detection and vetoes, while recovery and learning remain separate mechanisms. Memory Anchors shows how replay can support retention, with relevant past data and diversity still required. Evaluate the entire loop: productive work, interventions, resets and retry budgets, then improvement on the targeted failures and regression on earlier tasks. The strategic advantage is a repeatable, costed process that converts deployment evidence into better retained behavior.

The manuscripts distinguish the artifact that changes. PhysCaP updates physical beliefs and control programs without neural training; ASPIRE retains code and repair guidance; HARBOR and ENPIRE organize numerical policy-improvement experiments. EmbodiedSWE supplies verified simulation demonstrations for VLA fine-tuning.

The synthesis identifies the agent’s role and the human or engineered support around it. ASPIRE still needs real-world guidance and debugging; ENPIRE assumes prepared reset and verification interfaces; HARBOR’s gates do not guarantee semantic correctness. MobiAgent’s finite policy-update rounds plateau. These are useful improvements with stated limits, not evidence of unlimited recursive improvement.
